hook: Judea Pearl earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the Technion in Israel in 1960, then went on to complete master's degrees in electronics and physics in the United States before earning a PhD in electrical engineering from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn in 1965. He joined the computer science faculty at UCLA in 1969 and later founded its Cognitive Systems Laboratory. In the 1980s Pearl developed Bayesian networks, a mathematical framework for representing and reasoning about uncertain relationships among many variables, set out in his 1988 monograph Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems, which reshaped how artificial intelligence systems handle uncertainty. He then turned to an even harder problem, building a formal calculus, including what he called the do-calculus, for distinguishing genuine causation from mere correlation using data, work collected in his 2000 book Causality. He later explained these ideas for a general audience in The Book of Why, published in 2018. For this body of work he received the ACM A.M. Turing Award in 2011.

quick_facts: Earned a PhD in electrical engineering from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn in 1965
Joined the UCLA computer science faculty in 1969 and later founded its Cognitive Systems Laboratory
Developed Bayesian networks, set out in his 1988 monograph Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems
Built the do-calculus and structural causal models described in his 2000 book Causality
Won the ACM A.M. Turing Award in 2011 for contributions to probabilistic and causal reasoning in AI
Wrote The Book of Why in 2018 to explain causal reasoning for a general audience

achievements.title: Bayesian networks, 1988
achievements.impact: Introduced in his monograph Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems, this framework gave artificial intelligence a rigorous way to represent and update beliefs about uncertain, interrelated variables, and became foundational to modern probabilistic AI.

achievements.title: Do-calculus and structural causal models, described in Causality, 2000
achievements.impact: Provided formal mathematical tools for determining when cause and effect can be inferred from data, giving researchers across science and policy a rigorous alternative to relying on correlation alone.

achievements.title: ACM A.M. Turing Award, 2011
achievements.impact: Awarded for fundamental contributions to artificial intelligence through the development of a calculus for probabilistic and causal reasoning.

achievements.title: The Book of Why, 2018
achievements.impact: Brought decades of research on causal inference to a general readership, arguing that machines and scientists alike need explicit causal models, not just statistical correlation, to reason well.
